```ts
import type { TaskRef } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export const privateNotesSource: AcquisitionSource = {
	key: "private-notes",
	mode: "one",
	fields: ["notes"],
	access: "tasks:read-notes",
	accessUnknown: "wait",
	async run(request, context) {
		const target = request.identity as TaskRef;
		const response = await fetch(
			`/api/tasks/${encodeURIComponent(target.id)}/notes`,
			{ signal: context.signal },
		);
		if (!response.ok)
			throw new Error(`Notes request failed (${response.status}).`);
		const body: { notes: string } = await response.json();
		return {
			facts: [
				{
					resource: "tasks",
					identity: target,
					values: { notes: body.notes },
					basis: ["public"],
				},
			],
		};
	},
};
```


The list advertises only its public fields. The notes source controls whether that request can start; the resource's field rule protects the resulting notes. A source declaration describes capability, not proof that a request succeeded or permission was granted.

</details>

Known denial blocks an attempt. Unknown authority permits a source attempt by default; `accessUnknown: "wait"` waits for an independently established decision. A pure `(request, context) => "wait" | "attempt"` can distinguish caller discovery from a resource permission the endpoint itself establishes. Keep the actual permission in `access`. Use `available` for backend feature support, not authorization.

An editor's `prepare` function inherits the actual writable representation's proof with `context.disclosure({ resource, identity, field })`. The [editor example](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits#acquire-a-writable-baseline) shows this mapping. It does not rebuild permission generations. When draft fields have different evidence, `fieldDisclosure` overrides the common proof for those fields.

## 4. Change authority explicitly


```ts
export function withdrawNotes(runtime: Runtime) {
	runtime.revoke("tasks:read-notes");
}
export function leaveAccount(runtime: Runtime) {
	runtime.setAccess({
		contextId: "anonymous",
		decisions: [],
		retirePrevious: true,
	});
}
```


Losing the last read permission forgets the affected facts and managed draft values. Losing only write access disables saving while readable input remains. Changing caller retires that caller's authority; independently permitted information and public consumers survive.

Regrant permits new evidence. It does not restore forgotten values or make a retired response valid again. Keep asynchronous observations attached to their acquisition context. Losing visibility of an action does not prove accepted server work was canceled.

## When the response supplies more specific evidence

Most definitions use the rules above. A response may also reveal an independent invitation, an owning project, or other facts that determine why its information is readable.

<details>
<summary>Combine independent permissions on returned evidence</summary>

`basis` records why a returned fact may be disclosed. The resource's field rule remains an additional requirement. Capture response-specific evidence with `context.proof`:


```ts
import type {
	FactObservation,
	ResourceContext,
} from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import type { TaskRecord } from "../task-board/domain.js";

export function sharedNotes(
	task: TaskRecord,
	context: ResourceContext,
): FactObservation {
	return {
		resource: "tasks",
		identity: { id: task.id },
		values: { notes: task.notes },
		basis: [
			context.proof({
				all: ["signed-in", { any: ["team-member", "direct-invitation"] }],
			}),
		],
	};
}
```


Here sign-in is required, and either team membership or a direct invitation suffices. Withdrawing team access preserves the notes while the invitation remains valid. Withdrawing sign-in removes them.

A response can establish permissions and information together: return verified `grants` and a symbolic basis such as `basis: [{ all: ["signed-in", "tasks:read-notes"] }]` in the same observation batch. The acquisition context resolves the names after that batch's decisions, while fencing retired authority. Include only grants the response proves.

Entries in the `basis` array are independent alternatives. Memberships and relationships also carry evidence; [per-target relationship permissions](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/events#record-a-relationship-when-links-matter) use `targetBasis`. Use `public` only for permanently readable information. Publicly listed information that can become private needs a revocable permission.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Bind a permission to a project discovered later</summary>

Return this binding in the response's `grants` alongside its facts:


```ts
import type { AccessDecision } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";

export function taskReadBinding(
	taskId: string,
	projectId: string,
): AccessDecision {
	return {
		scope: `tasks:${taskId}:read`,
		requires: {
			all: [`projects:${projectId}:view`, `projects:${projectId}:tasks:view`],
		},
	};
}
```


It declares a dependency, not a grant. Add `state: "allowed"` only if the response verifies permission. Known denial of a prerequisite retires the dependent permission and its evidence. Unknown authority does not revoke existing evidence.

The first binding preserves currently permitted information; changing an established binding retires its old generation. A verified response can establish the new permission and data together. Saved bindings restore before protected payloads become visible. Every persistence adapter implements `writeAccessBindings`, even when its current binding set is empty. Failures are reported and block further protected payload writes while permitted live data remains usable.

</details>

Try [selective withdrawal](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/access). [Recovery](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/recovery) explains restoration and durable erasure.


---

# Configure the browser host

Connect a React app and its tabs to one shared owner.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host


This is application setup. Once it is in place, feature components only use the resource contract and hooks.

The **tab** renders UI. A **SharedWorker** runs the domain definitions, makes requests, receives events, and owns shared data. Both use the same pure read rules so filtering already-known data is immediate.

### Three responsibilities

1. Describe what the view needs. Render it with public hooks.
2. Define how backend responses, permissions, and operations work.
3. Connect tabs to one owner, with events and optional storage.

The tab holds a read model for synchronous rendering. The SharedWorker owns acquisition and mutation. Pure read definitions run in both places; credentials and HTTP stay in the owner integration.

## 1. Agree on compatibility

Share this object between your worker and tab modules:


```tsx
import { protocolVersion } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/client";
import { persistenceSchemaVersion } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
export const compatibility = {
	protocol: protocolVersion,
	schema: persistenceSchemaVersion,
	definitions: 1,
	build: "task-board-1",
};
```


Keep `definitions` unchanged for compatible domain edits; increment it when old and new definitions cannot safely share knowledge. `build` identifies the deployment. A different build alone does not require separate owners.

## 2. Start the owner

The worker imports the assembled owner definition as `taskDefinition`. This runnable task service emits full task updates on `task-events`; its facts declare that matching channel. Start with [resource sources](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources), then add the event decoder and [commands and edits](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits) your backend supports. The shared compatibility object is the one above:


```ts
import { createRuntime, DexiePersistence } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import { createSharedHost } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/worker";
import { compatibility } from "./compatibility.js";
import { taskDefinition } from "./domain.js";

const attach = createSharedHost({
	compatibility,
	lockName: "vem-task-board-owner",
	locks: navigator.locks,
	async create() {
		const client = createRuntime({
			resources: [taskDefinition],
			persistence: new DexiePersistence("vem-data:task-board:v1"),
		});
		const events = new EventSource("/api/events");
		events.onmessage = (event) => {
			try {
				client.event("tasks", JSON.parse(event.data));
			} catch (error) {
				console.error("Invalid task event", error);
			}
		};
		await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
			events.onopen = () => {
				client.setContinuity({ channel: "task-events" }, "live");
				resolve();
			};
			events.onerror = () => {
				client.setContinuity({ channel: "task-events" }, "interrupted");
				resolve();
			};
		});
		return {
			client,
			dispose() {
				events.close();
				client.close();
			},
		};
	},
});
const scope = globalThis as unknown as {
	onconnect: (event: MessageEvent) => void;
};
scope.onconnect = (event) => {
	for (const port of event.ports) void attach.then((connect) => connect(port));
};
```


`/api/events` is this example's backend event stream. Adapt its URL and event decoder to your service. This fixture sends full task updates. `setContinuity` reports whether that channel is continuously delivering them; a normal incoming update goes through `client.event`.

The starter waits for the initial event connection to open or fail before admitting readers. This keeps a late startup coverage change from making the first request obsolete. On failure, readers can still acquire snapshots. Reconnecting does not make observations from the uncovered interval current; affected active consumers need new evidence. Give the event transport a connection deadline if it can remain silent indefinitely.

Publish the worker at a stable URL, such as `/task-owner.js`, and keep the lock name stable across deployments. Changing the lock name for each release could allow two owners to run at once.

## 3. Connect the tab and provide the client

Pass the same `taskRead` rules used by the owner. `ownerModule` is the URL of the compiled worker module, served from the application's origin.


```tsx
import { connectSharedWorker } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/client";
import { taskRead } from "../task-board/read.js";

export function connectTasks(ownerModule: URL) {
	return connectSharedWorker(ownerModule, compatibility, {
		readDefinitions: [taskRead],
	});
}
```


Create the client once in the application entry point, then pass it into this provider. The browser needs HTTPS or loopback, SharedWorker, and Web Locks. Connection failures are application-level errors, separate from an individual query's failure.


```tsx
import type { BrowserClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/client";
import { DataProvider } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { type ReactNode, useSyncExternalStore } from "react";

export function TaskProvider({
	client,
	children,
}: {
	client: BrowserClient;
	children: ReactNode;
}) {
	const connection = useSyncExternalStore(
		client.subscribe,
		client.connectionSnapshot,
	);
	if (connection.phase === "connecting") return <p>Connecting…</p>;
	if (connection.phase !== "ready") {
		return (
			<p role="alert">{connection.error ?? "Reconnect to the task service."}</p>
		);
	}
	return <DataProvider client={client}>{children}</DataProvider>;
}
```


Put your routes inside the provider. Close the client when the app is permanently disposed; do not recreate it on route changes.

## Decide what survives a restart

Storage is optional: omit `persistence` for an in-memory owner. With `DexiePersistence`, a definition's `persist` decides which fields can be saved. For example, the task definition allows `$presence`, `title`, and `status`, and leaves private notes out. Relationships have a separate `persistRelationship` allowance. The starter uses the explicit IndexedDB name `vem-data:task-board:v1`; the constructor uses that name directly. Choose a namespace your application owns.

`runtime.ready` means restoration was attempted. It does not grant permission to show protected data. Establish the current caller through [access decisions](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/access); protected saved data stays quarantined until then. Report persistence errors through `RuntimeOptions.onError`, and inspect `action.recovery` before promising restart recovery.

## Let the browser continue an upload

This optional host integration uses Background Fetch where available. Commands declare their HTTP transfer; feature components keep using `useCommand` and `useAction`. Configure three cooperating pieces once per application:

| Where | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| SharedWorker | Runs the action, prepares the request, and interprets its result |
| Page | Initiates the browser transfer after the ServiceWorker admits the handoff |
| ServiceWorker | Atomically claims the protected action and stores its completion receipt |

The owner and ServiceWorker must use the **same Dexie database** as the action journal. All three use the same channel name. Keep both names stable across compatible deployments:


```ts
export const transferHost = {
	databaseName: "vem-data:task-board:v1",
	channel: "task-board-transfers-v1",
};
```


**In the SharedWorker**, use this factory from the existing `createSharedHost({ create })` callback. Retain your domain event connection and close it in the same `dispose` function:


```ts
import {
	createRuntime,
	DexiePersistence,
	type ResourceDefinition,
} from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import { createBackgroundTransfers } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/worker";
import { transferHost } from "./transfer-config.js";

export function createUploadOwner(resources: readonly ResourceDefinition[]) {
	const transfers = createBackgroundTransfers(transferHost);
	const client = createRuntime({
		resources,
		persistence: new DexiePersistence(transferHost.databaseName),
		transfers,
	});
	return {
		client,
		dispose() {
			client.close();
			transfers.close();
		},
	};
}
```


**In the application entry point**, call `connectUploadHost()` once. Keep the returned cleanup function for permanent application disposal:


```ts
import { attachBackgroundTransfers } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/client";
import { transferHost } from "./transfer-config.js";

export function connectUploadHost() {
	return attachBackgroundTransfers({
		serviceWorker: "/transfer-service-worker.js",
		scope: "/",
		channel: transferHost.channel,
	});
}
```


**In `/transfer-service-worker.js`**, compiled from this module:


```ts
import { installBackgroundTransfers } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/worker";
import { transferHost } from "./transfer-config.js";

installBackgroundTransfers(transferHost);
```


Serve this worker from your own origin with an appropriate scope. The example uses the origin root; an application under a subpath should use that subpath for both URL and scope. If the application already registers a ServiceWorker, install the handlers in that worker instead of creating a competing registration. This integration does not install a cache or intercept ordinary requests.

The native host accepts HTTP `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` uploads with a `Blob` body and a small text response. The [transfer definition](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits#declare-an-http-upload) describes the backend contract. Browser support, storage, and permission can prevent handoff; display the action's actual [execution lifetime](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/recovery#uploads-and-background-transfers), not a promise inferred from API availability.

<details>
<summary>Handle an application update</summary>

A compatible client can report `connection.updateAvailable`. To offer an update button:


```tsx
export async function updateApp(client: BrowserClient) {
	const update = await client.upgrade();
	if (update.ready) location.reload();
	return update.reason;
}
```


Display the returned reason if the owner refuses, for example because work is active or storage could not be flushed. An incompatible connection cannot use the old owner; ask the user to finish work in older tabs and close them before reopening. Never bypass this by inventing another lock name.

</details>

Next: [move progress from the page into shared feedback](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/feedback).


---

# Keep progress visible after navigation

Wire inline progress and shared notices once in the application shell.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/feedback


A task is still completing when its page closes. Its progress should move into a notice, then return inline if the page opens again. The owner decides which tab should show that notice; the application decides how it looks.

## Mark the inline surface

Use a shared page component to claim feedback for its query. The effect returns the release function, so navigating away automatically ends the claim.


```tsx
import type { BrowserClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/client";
import { useQuery } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { useEffect } from "react";
import { tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function TaskPageProgress({ client }: { client: BrowserClient }) {
	const result = useQuery(tasks.list({ select: ["title", "status"] }));
	useEffect(
		() =>
			client.claimQueryFeedback(tasks.list({ select: ["title", "status"] })),
		[client],
	);
	return (
		<div aria-live="polite">
			{result.activities.map((action) => (
				<p key={action.id}>
					{action.outcome?.kind ?? action.progress?.message ?? "Working…"}
				</p>
			))}
		</div>
	);
}
```


Mount this alongside the task list while the route is open. A scoped page should claim that same scope. Individual action buttons do not need to manage ownership.

## Render the shell's notices

Mount this component once inside `DataProvider`, outside the route content. `useActivities` reads shared action records; `client.feedback()` returns the IDs assigned to this tab for unsolicited feedback.


```tsx
import { useActivities } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { useSyncExternalStore } from "react";

export function ActionNotices({ client }: { client: BrowserClient }) {
	const ids = useSyncExternalStore(client.subscribe, client.feedback);
	const activities = useActivities();
	return (
		<aside aria-label="Activity" aria-live="polite">
			{activities
				.filter((action) => ids.includes(action.id))
				.map((action) => (
					<div key={action.id}>
						<span>
							{action.outcome?.kind ?? action.progress?.message ?? "Working…"}
						</span>
						<button
							type="button"
							onClick={() => client.acknowledgeFeedback(action.id, action)}
						>
							Dismiss
						</button>
					</div>
				))}
		</aside>
	);
}
```


This deliberately plain renderer shows the wiring. Replace its markup with your toast component and map outcome names to your application's messages.

Pass the displayed action snapshot to `acknowledgeFeedback`. That acknowledges the stage the user saw: dismissing a running notice will not accidentally dismiss a later failure.

## What happens in another tab?

The tab that started the action receives unsolicited feedback. If it closes, a surviving connected tab takes responsibility. Other tabs may still display related progress inline. Dismissal changes presentation; it never cancels accepted server work.

For a surface that has action IDs rather than a query, `claimFeedback(ids)` provides the same claim/release lifecycle. Test navigation and closing the originating tab in your application's browser tests.


---

# How Vem chooses reads

Declare backend capabilities; Vem plans across the whole outstanding demand.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/planning


**Vem chooses the reads. You describe what each source can provide.** There is no planner to write for a screen, resource, or combination of tabs.

A source is one supported way to read your backend: a URL list, a summary collection, one full record, a filtered search, or a page. It declares what information that read can establish and how to execute it.

## Plan for the whole application

The shared owner combines the currently outstanding query requirements it knows about, from every connected tab and imperative reader. It subtracts permitted information already known, expands prerequisites for derived fields, and compares combinations of available sources. Work already in flight can satisfy overlapping demand without another request. Later arrivals can reuse that work and its results; Vem does not predict requests from a tab that has not asked yet.

For example, four task details might be cheaper as one collection read. If three details are already known, one detail read might be cheaper. If another tab also needs collection membership, that changes the comparison again. No component chooses an endpoint.

### Experiment: One plan for several views

Open all task notes, then compare a single note after starting over. Explore sharing a pending reply and filtered pages.

Vem compares declared sources across the views that currently need information. Three task-note views can share a cheaper collection read; one view can use a detail read. A second view can join an in-flight fixed representation. A supported filter narrows acquisition, and the runtime follows pages until the actual response establishes completeness. The receipt counts real source calls to the simulated service.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

The receipt shows calls made by the runtime. The task views only ask for fields; none chooses the source.

### From need to knowledge

1. Collect what active consumers across tabs still need.
2. Subtract known facts and account for work already in flight.
3. Choose compatible reads using coverage, permissions, and cost.
4. Publish actual evidence, then plan for any remaining gaps.

The shared owner combines demand from tabs and imperative readers, subtracts known information, and reuses in-flight work. It compares declared backend capabilities and costs. Responses establish facts; missing information may require another source.

## Describe the alternatives

These two backend functions return observation batches, as shown in [Connect a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources). Their source declarations expose the choice to Vem:


```ts
import type {
	AcquisitionSource,
	ObservationBatch,
	ResourceContext,
} from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";

interface TaskReads {
	all(context: ResourceContext): Promise<ObservationBatch>;
	one(id: string, context: ResourceContext): Promise<ObservationBatch>;
}
export function taskSources(api: TaskReads): readonly AcquisitionSource[] {
	return [
		{
			key: "all-tasks",
			mode: "list",
			fields: ["title", "status", "notes"],
			membership: true,
			cost: 3,
			run: (_request, context) => api.all(context),
		},
		{
			key: "one-task",
			mode: "one",
			fields: ["title", "status", "notes"],
			cost: 1,
			run: (request, context) =>
				api.one((request.identity as { id: string }).id, context),
		},
	];
}
```


`key` names a backend source and must be unique within its resource. It is not a query cache key: Vem derives concrete request and query identities automatically. Screens do not define keys.

Register them as `sources: taskSources(api)` on the resource definition. The costs estimate the work of each acquisition, including expected pagination where applicable; they are relative values, not durations or guarantees. Both sources return fixed representations: one full task or all full tasks. Vem can use every returned field, even if the first consumer did not select it.

Vem compares acquisition sets using those estimates. It performs a bounded search, starting with a coverage-and-cost solution; when the search budget is reached it keeps the best solution found. This avoids an unbounded optimizer and does **not** promise a globally optimal plan for arbitrary backends. Describe meaningful cost differences rather than precise-looking guesses.

## Which characteristics belong in the definition?

| Capability | What Vem uses it for |
| --- | --- |
| `fields`, `relationships` | Identify which missing facts or links a read can supply |
| `membership` | Distinguish enumeration from details about already known records |
| `scope` | Keep tenant, project, or other collection boundaries separate |
| `filters` | Push supported equality terms to the backend; evaluate the remaining terms locally |
| `select: true` | Request only missing fields when the backend supports field selection |
| `cost` | Compare shared reads, smaller representations, and targeted requests |
| `pagination` | Follow bounded continuation without claiming an early page is complete |
| `access`, `accessUnknown` | Admit reads according to current authority before dispatch |
| `available` | Exclude a representation the backend does not support |

By default a source returns a fixed representation. With `select: true`, `request.fields` is the requested projection. Vem cannot expand a request already sent; a later field may require additional work. A fixed representation already in flight can serve any of its declared fields.

A URL, response header, or nested reference can establish facts too. Extract and advertise those facts when the backend semantics justify them. A URL containing a task ID may establish that ID; it does not establish permission, notes, or a writable representation's ETag.

<details>
<summary>When a collection returns only task URLs</summary>

Suppose a public endpoint returns the full list of URLs such as `/api/tasks/walk`. `load` below performs that request and checks its response. The task contract puts `id` in its resource reference, so this source can establish membership and presence without any display fields:


```ts
export function taskUrlSource(
	load: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<readonly string[]>,
): AcquisitionSource {
	return {
		key: "task-links",
		mode: "list",
		fields: [],
		membership: true,
		async run(_request, context) {
			const identities = (await load(context.signal)).map((href) => {
				const path = new URL(href, "https://tasks.example").pathname;
				const match = /^\/api\/tasks\/([^/]+)$/.exec(path);
				if (!match?.[1]) throw new Error("Unexpected task URL");
				return { id: decodeURIComponent(match[1]) };
			});
			return {
				facts: identities.map((identity) => ({
					resource: "tasks",
					identity,
					presence: "present",
					basis: ["public"],
				})),
				memberships: [
					{
						resource: "tasks",
						identities,
						complete: true,
						basis: ["public"],
					},
				],
			};
		},
	};
}
```


Add it alongside the other sources. Vem can use these known identities when choosing detail reads; this response supplies no title, status, or notes. If your contract also exposes an identity-derived field such as `name`, advertise it in `fields` and return its verified value in `values`.

This example's `complete: true` relies on the endpoint returning the whole visible collection. Use incomplete membership for partial responses. Preserve project or tenant context in both identity and scope when the URLs belong to separate collections.

</details>

## Filtering and pages

This source accepts a status filter and cursor pagination. The transport performs **one page**; Vem owns continuation:


```ts
interface TaskPage {
	tasks: Array<{ id: string; title: string; status: string }>;
	next?: string;
	complete: boolean;
}
export function pagedTasks(
	load: (url: URL, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<TaskPage>,
): AcquisitionSource {
	return {
		key: "task-pages",
		mode: "list",
		fields: ["title", "status"],
		membership: true,
		filters: ["status"],
		pagination: { pageSize: 50, maxPages: 20 },
		async run(request, context) {
			const url = new URL("/api/tasks", "https://tasks.example");
			if (request.where?.status)
				url.searchParams.set("status", String(request.where.status));
			url.searchParams.set("limit", String(request.page?.limit));
			if (request.page?.cursor)
				url.searchParams.set("cursor", String(request.page.cursor));
			const page = await load(url, context.signal);
			return {
				batch: {
					facts: page.tasks.map(({ id, ...values }) => ({
						resource: "tasks",
						identity: { id },
						values,
						presence: "present",
						basis: ["public"],
					})),
					memberships: [
						{
							resource: "tasks",
							where: request.where,
							identities: page.tasks.map(({ id }) => ({ id })),
							complete: page.complete,
							basis: ["public"],
						},
					],
				},
				next: page.next,
			};
		},
	};
}
```


`load` is your HTTP transport. `TaskPage.complete` reports whether the service established the final collection, including any partial-service failures. Vem accumulates page identities and keeps membership incomplete while continuation remains. A missing cursor is not, by itself, proof of completeness. Repeated cursors and page limits stop acquisition with an explanation; partial rows stay useful.

Pages may have different disclosure permissions. The accumulated collection is complete only while every contributing page’s evidence remains permitted; withdrawing a page’s permission preserves independently readable facts but removes that complete-set claim. Continuity combines across pages too: a complete set relies on every contributing page’s change coverage, while individual identities retain their own page’s support.

Only advertise filters with matching semantics. For declared equality filters, actual matching membership also establishes those field values: a task returned for `status: "open"` has that status even if the response omits the field. A broader response must supply or acquire the fields needed to evaluate the narrower filter locally. Filtering on the server may reduce payload without reducing server computation; model its cost accordingly. A complete result for `status: "open"` can support a stricter local filter, but cannot establish the entire unfiltered collection.

## Prerequisites and partial answers

Some reads require information first: for example, service capabilities determine which task representation exists. Declare that requirement with `readPrerequisites`:


```ts
import type { ResourceDefinition } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";

export const taskReadPrerequisites: ResourceDefinition["readPrerequisites"] =
	() => [
		{
			kind: "query",
			resource: "service",
			mode: "one",
			identity: "current",
			select: ["features"],
		},
	];
```


Install this as `readPrerequisites: taskReadPrerequisites` and register a `service` definition whose sources supply `features`. Vem shares that prerequisite acquisition across consumers, then chooses task sources from the updated knowledge. Already satisfied task queries keep using their data; this declaration does not introduce verification on each read. Failed, denied, or still-incomplete prerequisites settle with an explanation instead of dispatching the guarded source or retrying indefinitely.

Use `fieldDependencies` when a derived value needs other fields or related resources. These supply an alternative way to obtain a value, alongside sources that return it directly. It returns descriptions of the required information, using known identities or relationships; it does not fetch or choose endpoints. Vem includes those prerequisites in the shared plan and reevaluates them as evidence arrives. The existing `derive` function computes the value and reports its evidence dependencies. See [relationships and derived values](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/events).

A parent response can also establish another resource's existence or collection. Suppose a task detail includes its complete checklist. The checklist resource can declare a task-detail query through `membershipDependencies` for its list, or `presenceDependencies` for one item. Vem compares that route with direct checklist sources and can share a task read already needed elsewhere. The task response's extraction must still publish the checklist facts and scoped membership; a dependency declaration alone proves nothing. These callbacks return the same query or relationship descriptions as `fieldDependencies`, without orchestrating requests.

A source's declaration is a capability, not evidence. If a response omits fields or contains only part of a collection, publish exactly that. Vem can try another eligible source, then settles with the remaining gaps. It does not repeatedly request an unavailable field until it appears. Retry begins a new attempt; ordinary data has no time-based expiry.

Next: [connect permissions](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/access), or [apply events without unnecessary reads](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/events).


---

# Inspect consumers and try UI scenarios

Connect development tools to the same public contract your features use.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/devtools


Use **live inspection** to understand what a mounted screen requests. Use **scenarios** to see how that screen handles missing data, denied access, or a failed command. The choice belongs to the development host, not the feature component.

## Inspect a real screen

`inspectClient` from `/devtools` returns a wrapper. Pass `inspection.client` to `DataProvider`; mount your panel against `inspection.subscribe` and `inspection.getSnapshot`. Only consumers using that wrapper appear in the inspection.


```ts
import type { DataClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data";
import { inspectClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/devtools";
export function inspectDevelopmentClient(client: DataClient) {
	const inspection = inspectClient(client);
	return inspection;
}
```


The snapshot includes active queries, commands, editors, and actions. Inspection observes existing consumers; it does not fetch extra data. Call `inspection.close()` when removing the panel to detach inspection without closing the real client.

## Give the screen controlled data

A scenario catalog supplies example values and useful choices. The catalog is checked against the resource contract:


```ts
import {
	createScenarioClient,
	defineScenarios,
} from "@hyecompany/vem-data/devtools";
import { firstTask, tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function createTaskScenarios() {
	return createScenarioClient({
		resources: [
			defineScenarios(tasks, {
				example: {
					identity: firstTask,
					data: {
						title: "Plan a weekend walk",
						status: "open",
						notes: "Meet at 10.",
					},
				},
				fields: { status: { choices: ["open", "done"] } },
				commands: { complete: { outcome: { kind: "succeeded" } } },
				edits: { notes: { values: { notes: "Meet at 10." } } },
			}),
		],
	});
}
```


Pass the returned `scenario.client` to the same `DataProvider` used by the real application. It runs an isolated runtime instead of sending commands to your server.

Once a screen is mounted, a panel can change its discovered query:


```ts
import type { ScenarioClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/devtools";

export function showMissingTitles(scenario: ScenarioClient) {
	const query = scenario
		.getSnapshot()
		.queries.find(
			(item) => item.descriptor.resource === "tasks" && item.subscribers > 0,
		);
	if (query)
		scenario.setQuery(query.id, { state: "partial", missing: ["title"] });
}
```


The screen should keep the known row and show its missing title. Other query states are `ready`, `loading`, `empty`, `failed`, and `denied`. `setCommand` and `setEdit` control operation and editor scenarios. Call `scenario.close()` on disposal; recreate it for a full reset.

## Keep the integration in development

For a Vite application, use a build-time branch and a separate development module:


```ts
import type { DataClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data";
export async function prepareClient(client: DataClient) {
	if (import.meta.env.DEV) {
		const { inspectDevelopmentClient } = await import("./devtools.js");
		const inspection = inspectDevelopmentClient(client);
		return { client: inspection.client, inspection };
	}
	return { client };
}
```


The `devtools.js` module above exports `inspectDevelopmentClient`. Pass the returned client into the provider and the optional inspection into your panel. With other build tools, use their equivalent compile-time development entry point.

Place the panel in your existing developer-tools surface, such as TanStack Devtools. Vem supplies inspection and scenarios, not a bundled panel. Verify the final **client and worker** bundles exclude development imports and initialization; hiding the panel is not sufficient.


---

# Observe a server operation

Follow accepted work and recover without accidentally submitting it twice.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/operations


Some servers reply “accepted” while work continues in the background. A command's `run` should follow that work to its outcome. A recovered action should investigate the existing operation, not repeat the request that started it.

Use this adapter pattern only if your backend has equivalent semantics. **These endpoints are an example contract, not endpoints provided by Vem or the task-board demo.**

## The backend contract

| Request | Backend response |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /api/task-operations` with a task and action | HTTP 202 with `{ operationId: "op-42" }` |
| `GET /api/task-operations/op-42` | `{ state: "running" }`, `{ state: "succeeded", taskId: "walk" }`, or `{ state: "failed" }` |
| `GET /api/task-operations/op-42/wait` | Holds the request until the same operation reaches a terminal state |

Here success proves the named task is done. Failure is definitive, and this single-effect backend has no partial outcome. If your API can partly succeed, model that result explicitly. Missing history or a missing response proves neither success nor failure.

## Submit once, then checkpoint the receipt

Install `asynchronousCompletion()` as the resource's `commands.complete` definition. It uses the existing public `tasks.commands.complete(taskRef)` contract:


```ts
import type {
	ActionContext,
	ActionOutcome,
	CommandDefinition,
} from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";

export function asynchronousCompletion(
	request: typeof fetch = fetch,
): CommandDefinition {
	return {
		access: "public",
		disclosure: "public",
		recovery: () => ({}),
		async run(command, context) {
			const response = await request("/api/task-operations", {
				method: "POST",
				signal: context.signal,
				headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
				body: JSON.stringify({ task: command.target, action: "complete" }),
			});
			if (response.status !== 202) {
				return {
					kind: "unknown",
					message: "The service did not confirm acceptance.",
				};
			}
			const id = operationId(await response.json());
			if (!id)
				return {
					kind: "unknown",
					message: "The reply omitted its operation ID.",
				};
			await context.checkpoint({ operationId: id });
			context.submitted();
			return inspectOperation(id, context, request);
		},
		async recover(metadata, context) {
			const id = operationId(metadata);
			if (!id)
				return {
					kind: "unknown",
					message: "No operation ID was saved; investigate before retrying.",
				};
			return inspectOperation(id, context, request);
		},
	};
}
```


`recovery` supplies initial journal metadata before dispatch. Once acceptance provides an operation ID, `checkpoint` stores it. `submitted()` releases the submission slot so other commands can start while this one is monitored. The action remains running until `run` returns an outcome.

If storage fails, execution can continue but the action reports reduced recovery through `action.recovery`. Finishing `checkpoint()` is not, by itself, proof of durable storage. The host needs persistence configured before it can offer restart recovery.

## Observe the existing operation

Both initial execution and recovery use this function. It reads status once and, if necessary, waits on the backend's operation endpoint:


```ts
async function inspectOperation(
	id: string,
	context: ActionContext,
	request: typeof fetch,
): Promise<ActionOutcome> {
	const path = `/api/task-operations/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`;
	let response = await request(path, { signal: context.signal });
	if (!response.ok)
		return { kind: "unknown", message: "Operation history is unavailable." };
	let value: unknown = await response.json();
	if (hasState(value, "running")) {
		context.progress({ message: "The service is completing the task." });
		response = await request(`${path}/wait`, { signal: context.signal });
		if (!response.ok)
			return { kind: "unknown", message: "The final reply is unavailable." };
		value = await response.json();
	}
	if (
		hasState(value, "succeeded") &&
		"taskId" in value &&
		typeof value.taskId === "string"
	) {
		context.observe({
			facts: [
				{
					resource: "tasks",
					identity: { id: value.taskId },
					presence: "present",
					values: { status: "done" },
					basis: ["public"],
				},
			],
		});
		return { kind: "succeeded" };
	}
	if (hasState(value, "failed")) {
		return {
			kind: "failed",
			submitted: true,
			error: { message: "The service could not complete the task." },
		};
	}
	return {
		kind: "unknown",
		message: "The reply did not establish a final result.",
	};
}
```


There is no timer or ordinary-data refresh policy here. If your API offers operation events instead of a waiting endpoint, subscribe to that operation and settle from its terminal event. Closing a view is not cancellation of accepted work.

The final response updates the task through the action's context, so queries see the established status automatically. The sample treats non-202 submission replies conservatively; you may return a definite failure for response codes that your backend explicitly guarantees are rejections before any effect.

<details>
<summary>Response checks used in the example</summary>


```ts
function operationId(value: unknown): string | undefined {
	return typeof value === "object" &&
		value !== null &&
		"operationId" in value &&
		typeof value.operationId === "string" &&
		value.operationId.length > 0
		? value.operationId
		: undefined;
}
function hasState(
	value: unknown,
	state: string,
): value is Record<string, unknown> {
	return (
		typeof value === "object" &&
		value !== null &&
		"state" in value &&
		value.state === state
	);
}
```


These checks narrow the small example protocol. A production transport can use its normal schema validator for the same response shapes.

</details>

## What recovery can promise

Recovery uses the saved ID to call `GET` again. It never calls `POST`. If the ID was not durably recorded, or the backend discarded its history, the result stays unknown. That is a reason to investigate, not an instruction to retry automatically.

This sample does not implement backend cancellation or resumable uploads. For a [native transfer](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits#declare-an-http-upload), submitting a file and tracking the resulting operation are separate concerns: a journaled operation ID does not preserve the file's bytes, restart an interrupted upload, or guarantee the worker remains alive. Define those capabilities from the backend protocol before exposing them in the UI.

For how these actions stay visible across navigation, continue to [shared feedback](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/feedback). For owner lifetimes and restoration limits, see [ownership and recovery](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/recovery).


---

# Understand Vem

Follow the evidence behind acquisition, access, and recovery.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand



Read only the behavior you need to understand:

- [Shared knowledge and acquisition](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/acquisition): why known data is immediately useful and when a source read happens.
- [Access and disclosure](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/access): independent permissions, selective forgetting, and restoration.
- [Ownership and recovery](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/recovery): one owner, journaled actions, and uncertainty.

The [maintainer map](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/maintainer-map) links each explanation to implementation and behavioral tests.

# When Vem reads from the service

Reuse known information and acquire only what a view still needs.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/acquisition


Once a task list has loaded, filtering it should feel instant. Opening another view should reuse the same information. Try both in the app below.

### Experiment: Filter without fetching

Choose To do, open the overview, then open the walk’s notes.

Filtering and the overview reuse the task list. Opening notes asks for a missing field, so it reads once more. Returning to that detail reuses the new information.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

## A query describes a need

Vem first projects information it already knows and is allowed to show. Vem combines missing requirements across active consumers, including other tabs, and chooses among the backend capabilities declared by the integration. One response may satisfy several views; existing or in-flight information changes what is worth reading.

### From need to knowledge

1. Collect what active consumers across tabs still need.
2. Subtract known facts and account for work already in flight.
3. Choose compatible reads using coverage, permissions, and cost.
4. Publish actual evidence, then plan for any remaining gaps.

The shared owner combines demand from tabs and imperative readers, subtracts known information, and reuses in-flight work. It compares declared backend capabilities and costs. Responses establish facts; missing information may require another source.

## What is actually missing?

| The view needs… | What Vem must know |
| --- | --- |
| A list of tasks | Which tasks belong to the collection |
| Task titles | The selected field on each known task |
| Only unfinished tasks | Each candidate's status, even if status is not displayed |
| A definite empty state | Complete membership and enough information to evaluate the filter |

A missing title leaves a known task visible as an incomplete row. A missing status cannot establish whether a task matches the unfinished filter. [Partial results](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results) shows how to render both.

## A query is not a request cache key

Different queries can reuse the same facts. A list response that includes notes can satisfy a later notes view. If a detail response contains only one task's notes, opening a different task needs another read. The response's actual contents determine what becomes known.

To see Vem choose between competing reads across several views, try [the automatic planning example](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/planning#plan-for-the-whole-application).

The definition declares `sources`: available representations, fields, membership, supported filters, access, and relative cost. Vem plans automatically across the combined demand. [Connect a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources) shows the declarations; [how Vem chooses reads](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/planning) explains the selection and its bounds. Feature components only describe information.

## Is this field kept current?

Three questions stay separate: **may I see it**, **what was observed**, and **what keeps that observation current**. Permission answers the first; source responses answer the second; declared event continuity answers the third.

A task's status can be `live` while its notes are a `snapshot` from the last read. An `immutable` field needs no change monitoring because it cannot change for that identity. Vem reports these states per field; an open socket alone does not establish any of them.

Snapshots remain useful without automatic time-based verification. A known gap in the field's declared change coverage makes it stale and can require acquisition. A gap in another field's or project's channel does not. Domain authors [declare that coverage explicitly](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/events#declare-which-fields-the-events-keep-current).

## What makes Vem acquire again?

A new unsatisfied view, retrying unsuccessful acquisition, or a reported event-coverage gap can require new evidence. Mounting, focusing, or waiting a fixed time does not by itself make ordinary data expire.

Events can provide the missing values directly. When an older request finally returns, it cannot overwrite newer established observations or revive values under retired permissions.

<details>
<summary>Measurements that intentionally repeat</summary>

Measurements such as CPU usage are different from ordinary task data. A query can explicitly request a sample interval:


```ts
import { defineResource } from "@hyecompany/vem-data";

export const machines = defineResource<{ usage: number }, { id: string }>()({
	name: "machines",
	fields: ["usage"],
});
export const measuredUsage = machines.get(
	{ id: "web" },
	{
		select: ["usage"],
		sample: { fields: ["usage"], intervalMs: 1000 },
	},
);
```


Import `defineResource` from `@hyecompany/vem-data`. Subscribe with `useQuery(measuredUsage)`. The host also needs a `machines` definition that acquires usage. Sampled fields must be selected; intervals must be finite and at least 100 ms. Sampling ends when consumer demand ends, and does not make unrelated data expire.

</details>

## Why reload might make no request

A reloaded tab can rejoin an owner that still has the needed information. If the owner stopped, a new one can restore eligible data. Permitted values remain displayable, but non-immutable evidence—including plain snapshots—restores stale and the first active need reacquires it. Genuine immutable evidence can survive without another read. This re-establishes evidence after owner loss; it is not a mount, focus, or time-based policy. The integration also establishes the new owner's event continuity. Look at the owner's connection and coverage, not only the page reload, when diagnosing a missing request.


---

# Why information disappears after an access change

Keep readable information and forget only what lost its permission.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/access


A task's title can be public while its notes are private. You might be able to read those notes because you belong to a team, because you were invited directly, or both. Try removing each permission.

### Experiment: Who can still read the notes?

Turn off Team access, then the direct invitation.

Either permission can disclose the same private note. Losing both removes the note while the public task survives. A reply captured before withdrawal cannot restore that note after regrant; a new authorized update can.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

## A value can have more than one permission

Vem keeps the reasons a value may be shown alongside the value. The domain calls these its **disclosure bases**. If either team access or a direct invitation permits the notes, losing just one should not remove them.

| Change | Visible result |
| --- | --- |
| Team access ends; the invitation remains | Notes remain readable |
| The last permission ends | Notes disappear, including from managed edit drafts |
| Write permission ends, but read access remains | The draft stays; saving is disabled |
| Access is granted again | New authorized evidence can restore the notes |

Derived values and relationships also depend on the information and permissions supporting them. A total computed from unreadable records must not remain visible merely because the total was computed earlier.

## Unknown is different from denied

A fresh owner may not yet know who the caller is. Protected restored data stays hidden until the host establishes access. That uncertainty is not proof that permission was revoked.

Likewise, a network error during an established session is not a logout. Only an actual access decision or authority retirement withdraws the old permission. A logout can retire private access while leaving public data and the runtime alive.

## An old reply cannot undo withdrawal

A pending read carries the permission generation under which it started. If that permission is retired, the late response cannot repopulate protected data—even if access was granted again in the meantime. Regrant permits new evidence, not reuse of the retired response.

With persistence, Vem records revocation before deleting saved payloads. Live values disappear immediately even if storage fails; the failure must still be reported because durable cleanup was not established.

To implement these rules, follow [access controls step by step](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/access). Components should render managed query and edit values directly: independent copies in React state or a form library need their own withdrawal integration.


---

# What happens when the app closes mid-operation

Keep accepted work separate from what the UI knows about it.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/recovery


An app can close after sending a command but before learning what happened. Sending it again could repeat work. Try returning to an unfinished task below.

### Experiment: Return to an unfinished action

Complete the walk, then close and reopen the example.

The first owner records possible submission and sends once. A replacement owner restores its journal and investigates. Missing confirmation leaves the result unknown; recovery never resubmits the command.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

## Sending, watching, and showing are separate

| What happened | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| You navigate away | The shared owner can continue observing the action |
| You dismiss its notice | Feedback is acknowledged; server work is unchanged |
| You lose permission to see it | Protected details disappear; accepted work may continue |
| The owner stops before receiving a result | The next owner needs evidence before deciding what happened |

## Recovery investigates

When storage works, Vem records that submission may occur **before** dispatch. An operation ID returned by the backend can then be saved as recovery metadata. After interruption, the domain's `recover` function uses that metadata to check the backend's operation record.

### Recovery investigates what happened

1. Record possible submission before sending, when storage works.
2. A lost response does not tell us whether the work happened.
3. Restore the action record after access is established.
4. Check what happened. Do not send the command again.

A missing response, missing journal, or missing operation history does not prove that the operation never happened. Recovery is not an instruction to submit again. A lock protects owner exclusivity; a heartbeat timeout cannot transfer ownership.

If the operation record proves success, recovery may report success. If the record is absent or no useful metadata survived, the truthful outcome may be `unknown`. Missing history is not proof that no work occurred. Recovery must not simply call the command again.

The [command implementation guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits) explains submission and checkpoints. The embedded example intentionally returns an uncertain result so you can see this boundary.

## Storage failure reduces recovery

Actions can still execute if storage fails. Their `recovery` state is then `unavailable`; display that limitation where a user is relying on restart recovery. `RuntimeOptions.onError` receives owner errors such as persistence failures.

## Uploads and background transfers

A command can declare a native HTTP `transfer`. With the [browser transfer host](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host#let-the-browser-continue-an-upload), the browser can accept responsibility for moving its bytes after tabs close. Without that integration, or when the browser cannot use it, the SharedWorker sends the request while the application remains open.

| Action state | What the UI can say |
| --- | --- |
| `execution.lifetime === "owner"` | Keep an application tab open; show `execution.reason` when present |
| `execution.lifetime === "browser"` | The browser accepted the transfer; closing this tab does not itself cancel it |
| `recovery === "saved"` | The action checkpoint was saved; this alone says nothing about who owns the request |

API support alone does not establish browser ownership. Vem reports `browser` only after an actual handoff acknowledgement or recovered evidence of acceptance. The browser may still stop the transfer, storage may fail, and the server may reject it. The [Background Fetch API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Background_Fetch_API) is not supported by Firefox or Safari; those browsers use the owner lifetime.

The ServiceWorker saves a bounded response receipt in the same protected journal. A returning owner uses that evidence or investigates the existing browser registration; it never starts a replacement upload. If the acknowledgement or result is missing, the outcome can remain `unknown`. A lost acknowledgement does not trigger an owner-bound fallback, because that could send the upload twice.

**Continuation is not resumption.** The journal does not contain the uploaded file, and Vem has no automatic upload replay. A resumable backend needs its own transfer identity and accepted-byte protocol. The [Background Fetch specification](https://wicg.github.io/background-fetch/) restricts automatic request restart to GET because repeating other methods can cause side effects.

The browser uses the request's credential policy; the journal does not pin a cookie, TLS identity, or authenticated session. Credentials can change while work is pending. Server authorization remains authoritative. Read-access loss removes protected activity and receipts; losing write access blocks a handoff that has not started, but does not mean already accepted work was canceled. Explicit cancellation can leave partial remote effects and must not be presented as rollback.

## One owner makes shared decisions

The SharedWorker owns acquisition, actions, and persistence. Tabs own views. A version-independent Web Lock protects ownership, including during updates. A delayed heartbeat does not authorize a second owner.

Use the [browser-host guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host) to configure that boundary. Runtime defaults bound concurrent reads and commands to four each; adjust concurrency and retention through [RuntimeOptions](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/api/runtime.Interface.RuntimeOptions) when your backend or application needs different limits.

# API map

Choose the public import for the responsibility you own.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/api-map



| Import | Audience | Main exports |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@hyecompany/vem-data` | Features and contracts | `defineResource`, `defineCommand`, `defineEdit`, `hasFields`, descriptions and result types |
| `@hyecompany/vem-data/react` | React features | `DataProvider`, `useQuery`, `useCommand`, `useEdit`, `useAction`, `useActivities`, `queryView` |
| `@hyecompany/vem-data/client` | Tab host | `connectSharedWorker`, `BrowserClient`, compatibility |
| `@hyecompany/vem-data/worker` | Owner bootstrap | `createSharedHost`, owner contract |
| `@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime` | Domain and owner integration | `createRuntime`, `ResourceDefinition`, evidence types, `DexiePersistence` |

[Browse all generated signatures](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/api), or search for an exact API name. Entry-point listings link every exported declaration, including its members and generic parameters. Shared types may be linked to their canonical declaration under another entry point.

Use only package exports. Internal stores, worker messages, and database rows are not the feature API. Low-level structural helpers `query`, `command`, and `edit` exist, but named resource contracts are the primary contributor interface.

# Troubleshooting

Start with what you see, then check the responsible layer.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/troubleshooting


## Nothing fetched or no event socket

- **In the embedded examples:** the service is simulated inside the page. The counter measures calls to that source, not HTTP requests.
- **In your application:** inspect the existing query's `issues` and whether its requested fields and membership are already known. A satisfied query needs no acquisition.
- **With a SharedWorker host:** inspect the worker's network activity. Page developer tools may not show its requests. Your host opens the event transport; Vem does not choose or open one automatically.

A failed HTTP request is not proof of logout. Check the source URL, proxy, and authentication separately. See [when acquisition happens](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/acquisition).

## Opening another task did not add a service read

The earlier response may have included both tasks' details. Vem reuses all established facts, not only those used by the first view. If it returned only one task, a missing detail on another task should cause acquisition. Check the response contents and your source declarations and response extraction before expecting one request per screen.

## Loading when changing a known filter

Check `readDefinitions` in `connectSharedWorker`: the tab needs the same pure read rules as the owner. Then check the filter fields and `confirmed.complete`. An unknown predicate or incomplete membership can require acquisition.

If the required information is present and permitted, a loading flash is a defect. Do not add a timer or a second feature cache to conceal it. [Browser setup](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host) shows the shared read definition.

## Partial rows or no confirmed total

A row's `missing` fields, unresolved filter candidates, and incomplete membership mean different things. Keep known rows visible. Only `confirmed.complete` establishes the matching set, and only `result.empty` proves emptiness. [Partial-result rendering](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results) provides the code.

## Save conflict

Confirm that the edit's ETag came from the same response as its baseline. Preserve the draft when the server rejects that token. Let the user reload explicitly; silently replacing the token would turn an old draft into an overwrite of someone else's changes. [Editor recipe](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/editors).

## Another tab has different behavior

Start with `client.connectionSnapshot()`. If it is not `ready`, address the reported connection error first. Then compare the tabs' origin, worker URL, and definitions version. Same-origin tabs must use the same ownership lock name across versions. [Host compatibility](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host#1-agree-on-compatibility).

## A failed action cannot be retried

Default retry requires a settled failure explicitly marked `submitted: false`, and excludes restored actions. A failed response after possible submission does not meet that rule. The domain can override retry only when backend evidence makes another attempt safe. [Command controls](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/actions).

## Data disappeared after an access change

Check whether the data lost its last allowed disclosure basis. If it did, disappearance is expected—even from an unsaved draft. Granting permission again allows new evidence; an old response cannot refill the values. [Implementing access](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/access) explains the declarations.

## Recovery is unavailable

Check `action.recovery` and the owner's `onError` reports for persistence failures. Execution can continue while restart recovery is reduced. If a command has no backend operation history to investigate, its journal cannot prove the outcome. [Recovery](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/recovery).


---

# Maintainer map

Trace a documented behavior to implementation and focused tests.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/maintainer-map



Paths below are relative to `packages/data`. Read the relevant guide first, then the implementation and behavioral tests. Internal paths are a navigation aid, not import recommendations.

| Behavior | Implementation | Test search |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typed descriptions and selected fields | `src/contracts.ts`, `src/descriptors.ts` | `tests/contracts/`, `tests/types/` |
| Query projection and partial membership | `src/read-model/`, `src/runtime/memberships.ts` | `tests/queries/`, `tests/knowledge/` |
| Missing-information acquisition | `src/runtime/acquisition.ts`, `src/runtime/planning*.ts`, `src/runtime/source-execution.ts`, `src/read-model/requirements.ts` | `tests/planning/` |
| Observations and dependencies | `src/runtime/knowledge.ts`, `src/runtime/relationships.ts` | `tests/knowledge/` |
| Access and restoration | `src/access.ts`, `src/access-proofs.ts`, `src/runtime/restoration.ts` | `tests/access/`, `tests/persistence/` |
| Actions and recovery | `src/actions.ts`, `src/actions/` | `tests/actions/`, `tests/persistence/recovery.test.ts` |
| Managed editing | `src/edit.ts`, `src/runtime/edit-admission.ts` | `tests/editing/` |
| Owner and tab publication | `src/worker.ts`, `src/client.ts`, `src/read-model/` | `tests/host/` |
| Persistence | `src/persistence.ts` | `tests/persistence/` |

The package also keeps liveness and query presentation checks in `tests/queries`, developer-tool checks in `tests/devtools`, and executable-example checks in `tests/examples`. Compile-only assertions in `tests/types/*.types.ts` run through type checking, not the runtime test runner.

At the repository root, `tests/docs` checks the built site, with focused learning tools in `tests/docs/experiments`. `tests/package` checks the actual HTTP/SharedWorker starter, including the packed independent consumer exercised by `scripts/check-package.mjs`. Helpers belong in the nearest `support` directory; only browser launch configuration shared by both suites lives in root `tests/support`.

Before changing a behavior, identify the public contract it affects and add or adjust a focused behavioral test. Keep generic owner and storage mechanics out of domain-specific feature additions.

## Trace a query update

The owner publishes permitted records and membership evidence. A tab applies that publication to its local read model and projects the queries its components use. The owner uses the same projection rules when deciding what information is still missing. Feature code does not manage either copy.

For an existing query, Vem retains each record's contribution: whether it matches, its displayed values, and its missing requirements. A record update recalculates that record's contribution. Unchanged records reuse their previous calculations. Custom scope and filter functions are evaluated again for a changed record; Vem does not assume that these functions read only selected fields.

Before projection, an ordinary observation recalculates currency for changed facts and facts whose evidence depends on them. The dependency index carries changes through derived facts and relationships; it does not treat a new value as evidence that unrelated facts changed. Access changes and event-continuity changes can require broader checks.

This saves repeated evaluation of every resource when one resource changes. Assembling a changed result can still depend on its row count. It is not a constant-time guarantee for every publication.

Access and membership changes can affect which records belong or may be disclosed, so they require broader recomputation. Initial attachment, reset, or a query falling behind the bounded change history can also rebuild its projection. These paths preserve the same results as a full calculation. Inactive retained queries do not perform notification work; reading them again catches up to the current model.

Start with `src/read-model/query-projector.ts` for query contributions, `src/read-model/projection.ts` for the tab's local model, and `src/runtime/read-model-export.ts` plus `src/read-model/publication.ts` for publication changes. Follow the behavior tests in `tests/host` and `tests/queries` before changing their bookkeeping.

## Measure the right work

Run from the repository root:

```sh
node --import tsx scripts/benchmarks/data-publication.mjs 100 1000 5000
node --import tsx scripts/benchmarks/publication-pipeline.mjs 100 1000 5000
```

The first isolates owner observation without active owner queries and tab projection. The second includes active owner queries and three simulated tabs, measuring delta preparation, structured cloning, replica application, and subscriber reads separately. It checks selected-field updates, movement between filters, and updates outside some selections.

These are CPU benchmarks with deterministic data. Their sum is not browser interaction latency: actual Worker scheduling, network, React, and rendering are excluded. Use a browser profile to assess those parts, and behavioral tests to assert which records are evaluated rather than machine-specific timing limits. `packages/data/tests/README.md` documents the benchmark settings and comparison options.


---

# Integration limits

Know which guarantees your backend and browser host must provide.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/limits


## Bound requests that may never return

Vem settles an acquisition when the source answers or fails. The runtime currently has no built-in deadline for a source promise that never settles. This is a gap in the intended finite-read guarantee: a hanging adapter can keep an imperative read pending.

Set transport deadlines in your domain integration. An imperative caller can also bound its own wait:


```ts
import type { DataClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data";
import { firstTask, tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";
export function readTaskWithDeadline(client: DataClient) {
	return client.read(tasks.get(firstTask, { select: ["title"] }), {
		signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
	});
}
```


`DataClient` comes from `@hyecompany/vem-data`; `tasks` is the application's resource contract. Catch an aborted read at the caller. Aborting withdraws that caller's demand, including reads queued before attachment. It does not cancel shared work needed by another view. An acquisition already in flight may finish and contribute permitted evidence; the abandoned reader does not request further acquisition.

## Automatic planning is bounded

Vem chooses acquisition sets from declared capabilities and current knowledge. It cannot infer undocumented backend semantics or know future demand. When record identities or related links are unknown, it may first acquire membership, then plan again with that evidence. Its cost estimates come from the integration; the bounded search keeps the best plan it finds, not a universal optimum.

`maxConcurrent` defaults to 4 source reads. `maxAcquisitionsPerRead` defaults to 4,096 dispatched sources per attempt; exhausting it leaves a partial result with an explanation. Paged sources default to at most 100 pages unless configured. Sources must provide transport deadlines and truthful completeness. These bounds prevent an unbounded acquisition loop; increase them deliberately for larger supported workloads.

## Match promises to your integration

| You want… | Your integration must provide… |
| --- | --- |
| Current data after a disconnected event stream | Accurate field/channel continuity and replay or reacquisition after a gap |
| Private fields to disappear on access loss | Accurate access decisions and disclosure bases |
| Conditional saves | A token from the same writable representation as the draft baseline |
| Recovery after the owner stops | Persistence plus backend evidence the domain can investigate |
| An upload that continues after tabs close | The [browser transfer host](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host#let-the-browser-continue-an-upload), durable storage, browser support, and confirmed handoff |
| A resumable transfer | A backend transfer protocol and enough durable metadata to resume it |
| Form-library values to be forgotten | Integration that withdraws its values and defaults alongside the edit session |

Vem provides the coordination contracts. It does not generate backend semantics from a schema or supply a form library, authorization server, upload protocol, or development panel.

## What the documentation examples exercise

The embedded examples run Vem against simulated services in the page. They demonstrate shared planning, per-field continuity, actions, access, and edits. Their counters do not represent HTTP traffic; their recovery example uses memory storage.

Repository integration checks separately exercise an actual SharedWorker, HTTP/events, conditional writes, and a packed independent consumer. Backend-specific behaviors still belong in your domain's tests. Use [feature fixtures](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/testing) for screens and [the resource guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources) for integration boundaries.


---

# Contribute to these docs

Keep guides, examples, reference, and exports in sync.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/contributing



## Update a guide

Edit `packages/docs/content/handbook`. Lead with the task and prerequisites, show a small useful example, explain the decisions the reader must make, and link a relevant next step. Add a page's title, description, and order in frontmatter. Navigation and machine-readable exports are generated from that content.

Run `npm run docs:prepare` after content changes, then `npm run docs:dev` to preview. Generated content in `content/docs`, `.generated`, and the static `out` artifact is not edited by hand. Source typechecking excludes the previous `out` artifact; the actual example files are compiled separately. During a running preview, rerun `docs:prepare` to publish source changes.

## Show executable code

Put runnable TypeScript in `packages/data/examples`, imported only through public package entries. Mark a focused region with `// #region name` and `// #endregion name`. Use an `Example` include with its file and optional region in a guide. The generator inserts that exact code. Include the code needed for the task on the page; a source link should never be required to understand an omitted step.

Compile examples with `npm run typecheck`. Add negative type assertions for important boundaries such as unselected fields, invalid command inputs, and proposal targets. Do not maintain a second hand-copied tutorial implementation.

## Add a diagram or experiment

Diagram content lives in `content/diagrams.json`. Each node keeps its title, icon, color, and short explanation together. Static diagrams should explain the whole relationship at a glance. Use interaction only when changing something teaches a behavior that a static picture cannot. Add an icon to the small map in `components/Flow.tsx` when needed.

Experiment prompts and explanations live in `content/experiments.json`; focused implementations live in `components/labs`. Start with one useful move the reader can make, then make its result easy to see. Keep technical scope and longer explanations in the expandable section.

The task board at `components/TaskBoardDemo.tsx` is a short, ordered walkthrough of the same lessons used in the guides. `components/lesson` owns the shared application view and teaching presentation, using shadcn components. `components/labs/sources` owns each controlled source. Both use public Vem APIs.

Give each lesson one familiar task first. Explain the observed result in one sentence, after the interaction. Keep unusual responses and permission changes in optional controls. Teach with the app, not a panel of internal state. Match the guide’s technical explanation to that experience, and verify the initial state as well as the failure paths.

Tutorial snippets are extracted from compiled files in `packages/data/examples`. Keep each excerpt focused, and show or explain the imports and local values it needs. The repository fixture separately checks HTTP and SharedWorker integration; running it is a contributor check, not a reader prerequisite. The in-page lessons use simulated calls, so never label their counters as HTTP traffic.

Each experiment needs an initial state, a few labeled controls, reset, observable results, and honest execution scope. Keep interaction user-controlled and keyboard accessible. Add browser checks for reset and meaningful failure paths. Avoid one combined control panel that requires learning every concept at once.

## Change the API reference

Update JSDoc on the public source declaration. `scripts/generate-reference.mjs` reads the package's seven export entry points through pinned TypeDoc and its Markdown plugin. Signatures and member lists are generated; semantic responsibilities belong in source comments and the relevant guide.

## Review the teaching value

Read the rendered page as someone doing the task for the first time. Can they tell where the code belongs, understand its inputs, and use its output without opening a source repository? Explain one practical default before introducing optional mechanisms. Remove repeated scope disclaimers, unexplained API lists, and controls that do not teach anything new.

## Validate the reader journeys

```sh
npm run check
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run test:package
npm run docs:build
npm run test:docs
```

For Pages, build with `BASE_PATH=/vem-web` in the environment. Check search, links and anchors, mobile width, zoom, keyboard focus, reduced motion, and ordinary reading with JavaScript disabled. Do not publish as a side effect of local validation.

`llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, and `docs.json` come from the same content. Text exports expand code excerpts and explain diagrams and experiments; they must not contain unresolved component tags.

For host development, `npm run example:dev` starts the repository's HTTP/event fixture and SharedWorker application on `http://127.0.0.1:4310`. Use it to investigate transport or cross-tab behavior. The learning examples remain embedded in the docs.


---

# Interface: Compatibility

# Function: defineCommand()

Generated from the public package entry points. Types and signatures follow the installed source.

***


> **defineCommand**\<`Input`, `Outcome`, `Target`\>(): [`CommandContract`](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference/api/index.Interface.CommandContract)\<`Input`, `Outcome`, `Target`\>

Declare a command input, supported outcome, and optional target type; this creates no execution.
